name: Cascadian Route
text: [approach_variants] The North Star-Bonanza col, then talus south to the white slabs beside the caret-shaped snowpatch.

[approach_variants] The descent from the Southwest Summit traverses to the Isella Glacier and follows an undulating line of steep rock and moraine at about two-thirds of the glacier's height, then crosses a notch in the south ridge back to the col camp — two ropes..
[approach_variants] A descent that crosses the Isella Glacier and a notch in the south ridge, needing two ropes and daylight.
[approach_variants] The first pitch begins at a small caret-shaped snowpatch, and you start just right of it.

[approach_variants] The negative marker is the strongest on this page, and it is about what lies further right: the part of the wall to the right of this route, above the long snowfield, is unclimbed, and the party who looked hardest at it described it as atrocious.
[approach_variants] This route begins just right of a tiny snowpatch, not above a long one.
[approach_variants] If you are standing under a big snowfield, keep walking back left.
[gear] two ropes for the Isella Glacier descent

[descent] Descend via the Isella Glacier, following a mostly continuous walkway of steep rock and mellow moraine at roughly two-thirds glacier height, then cross a notch in the south ridge back to base camp.

[descent_text] From the Southwest Summit, downclimb/traverse to the Isella Glacier and descend along an undulating line of steep rock and moraine at about two-thirds of the glacier's height, then cross through a notch in the south ridge to regain the North Star-Bonanza col c
[seasonal_guidance] Mid-August to mid-September, when the loose west face is driest and the high camp approach is snow-free.
[seasonal_guidance] Snow lingers on the approach to the North Star-Bonanza col camp and meltwater loosens the already chossy west face..
[seasonal_guidance] Early-season snow and freezing nights on a loose Grade V face where retreat near the summit roofs is difficult..
[pro_tips] The descent via the Isella Glacier's 'walkway' at roughly two-thirds height is the key to avoiding the worst of the glacier.
earlierWhy: why: Descent crosses the Isella Glacier on rock and moraine near its margin; ascent has snowpatches.
heldBecause: one account of the descent; the approach was assumed, not described

lastPage.why: An account of the climb and descent says the descent follows a rock and moraine walkway through the Isella Glacier without touching snow.

name: Standard Scramble
text: [seasonal_hazards] a slip on the exposed sections, serious routefinding error, or getting caught out on a lingering snowfield could require a lengthy, multi-day self-rescue given the long committing retreat.
[seasonal_hazards] N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble route climbed outside NWAC's winter avalanche forecast season.
[seasonal_hazards] N/A - no glacier travel on the Pulitzer scramble itself (unlike segments of the broader Bailey Range Traverse near Mount Olympus)
[overview] The standard line follows the east ridge (the 1961 first-ascent route), approached from a high camp in Ferry Basin or at Lone Tree Pass, over heather, snow, and talus.
[obj_haz] lingering snowfields/glacier remnants on approach.
[watch_out] snowfields.
[gear] ice axe.
[gear] crampons (early-season snowfields).
[rack] Glacier rope + crevasse-rescue hardware (Tibloc/Micro Traxion) for Bailey Range glacier crossings

[detailed_rack] Because Pulitzer is only reached via the Bailey Range Traverse, parties carry full glacier travel kit for the approach, including a glacier rope for crossing Bailey Range snowfields and glaciers such as the one on Pulitzer's own north slope and Humes Glacier f
[what_to_bring] crampons and ice axe — Bailey Range snowfields and glaciers on the approach.
[what_to_bring] crevasse-rescue hardware (e.g., Tibloc/Micro Traxion) — Bailey Range snowfields and glaciers on the approach

[bail] the only established ways off the range are the Elwha Snowfinger, Dodger Point, and Humes Glacier exits, all long and committing with no quick escape.

name: Northeast Ridge (Nason Ridge Traverse)
text: [beta] The finish of a longer cross-country ridge traverse rather than a stand-alone climb: from the Howard-Rock col, ascend Rock Mountain's northeast side (snow climbing and rock scrambling), then descend via the South Ridge-East Slope to the Rock Lake basin and exi
[beta] Requires solid off-trail navigation and, in early season, snow-travel skills (an ice axe was necessary on a June ascent).
[hazards] Sustained snow-climbing and rock-scrambling terrain across three summits.
[obj_haz] snow travel.
[watch_out] Snow conditions on the Mastiff/Howard/Rock ridges can require an ice axe and solid snow-travel skills even in June..
[gear] ice axe.
[approach] Howard's Northeast Ridge (both reported as snow climbs/rock scrambles) before dropping to the Howard-Rock col and climbing Rock Mountain's northeast side.
[turnaround] This is sustained, off-trail ridge terrain with snow-climbing sections in early season;

[turnaround] turn around or retreat over known ground if weather deteriorates or if snow conditions on the connecting ridges feel unstable, since there is no maintained trail to fall back on until the final descent to Rock Lake.
[seasonal_guidance] July through mid-September, after snow melts off the Mastiff and Howard ridges and before the first fall snow.
[seasonal_guidance] US 2 is open, but the connecting ridges are corniced snow and the slopes above Merritt Lake are still avalanche terrain..
[seasonal_guidance] Most ridge snow is gone and leftover patches are the only water on the crest;
[seasonal_guidance] Firm snow still covers the Mastiff and Howard ridges;
[seasonal_guidance] an ice axe and snow-travel skills are needed across the traverse..

round8: yes (text): The finish is described as snow climbing on the northeast side with firm ridge snow needing an axe.

name: West Ridge Scramble
text: [seasonal_hazards] No NWAC forecast covers the summer window, but the Tailgunner Couloir and north slope hold steep snow into early summer, and that snow can release wet slides on warm afternoons — climb it while it is firm..
[seasonal_hazards] wet-slide potential only where snow still lingers in the couloir early in the month.
[seasonal_hazards] Wet-slide potential on the couloir and north-slope snow during warm spells;
[seasonal_hazards] N/A - no glacier travel
[approach_variants] It passes a short waterfall ravine and reaches the couloir, which carries steep snow in spring and early summer.
[approach_variants] Steep, often corniced snow in the couloir and on the north slope into early summer.

[approach_variants] From there the climb goes west below Tailgunner's north side, up the north slope to the west ridge, then over a relic cornice headwall below the summit dome and a narrow summit ledge that is the crux and can be icy with snow lingering.
[beta] a narrow summit ledge is the crux and can be exposed or icy if snow lingers.

[beta] In late-spring snow conditions parties have instead cramponed up a north-slope snow route and surmounted a corniced west-ridge headwall — a more technical, roped variation not represented by the Class 3 rating.
[hazards] Steep, often corniced snow on the Tailgunner Couloir and north slope well into early summer.
[obj_haz] Wet-slide avalanche potential on the north-slope snow/couloir during warm spells.
[obj_haz] Remnant cornice/headwall on the west ridge that can hold snow into summer
[watch_out] Carry an ice axe and crampons if climbing before mid-July — the couloir and north slope hold snow long after the valley trail is dry.
[gear] ice axe.
earlierWhy: Text says no glacier; couloir/north slope hold steep snow into early summer, season starts June.
round8: yes (text): The couloir and north slope hold steep snow well into early summer, inside a June start, and a June report found a steep snow traverse with a cornice.

lastPage.why: A June report found the approach and slopes fully snow-covered with a cornice, and the couloir holds steep snow into early summer inside the June start.

name: Southwest Couloir
text: [overview] snow higher up is moderately steep and may need steps cut or kicked early in the season or day.
[descent] pass the saddle fully before turning east, because the snowfield northeast of it is steep early season
[descent_text] Go all the way past the saddle before turning east, because the snowfield northeast of it is steep early in the season.
[descent_text] Expect snow in early season and talus with some scrambling later, then follow the south fork of Garnet Canyon down to the Meadows and the trail.
